neighbours.label: the word just before a body part or tissue in text about a disease, pathogen or toxin harming the body ('attacks the', 'under the', 'in your')
fire: The bacteria slowly invade the lining of the stomach and cause ulcers.
Mercury from the fish gradually accumulates in the brain and nerves of children.
Ticks attach themselves under the skin and can pass on Lyme disease.
The measles virus first infects the lungs before spreading through the body.
Chronic exposure to arsenic damages the liver and the kidneys.
Rabies travels along the nerves until it reaches the spinal cord.
Untreated, the infection eats away at the bones of the jaw.
This fungus grows inside the lungs of people with weak immune systems.
quiet: The bacteria were first described by a Dutch scientist in the 1880s.
Mercury from the fish market is a common worry for coastal towns.
Ticks are most common in long grass during the warm summer months.
The measles vaccine is given to children in two doses before school.
Chronic exposure to arsenic is a public health issue in some regions.
Rabies is rare in the city, but vets still vaccinate every dog.
Untreated, the infection can last for many weeks and spread to others.
This fungus grows on old bread kept in a warm, damp kitchen.

notes: Peaks are function words (the, under, in, Attacks) right before a body part in disease/toxin passages. Near misses keep the medical topic but without a body-part slot, or put the slot in a harmless context.
